# 1 Samuel 19 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter presents four successive escapes of David from Saul's murderous intent: (1) through Jonathan's intervention (vv. 1–7); (2) by David's own agility dodging the spear (vv. 8–10); (3) through Michal's help (vv. 11–17); and (4) by the prophetic sanctuary at Naioth under Samuel (vv. 18–24). Precept Austin notes a three-part outline: Jonathan protects David, Michal protects David, Samuel protects David—yet in reality it is the Spirit of God who is David's true Protector throughout. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-19-commentary)

---

## v. 1 — Saul Orders David's Death; Jonathan's Love

**Traditional reading:** Saul now openly commands Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. This marks a new stage in Saul's descent — he has moved from secret scheming and hoping the Philistines will kill David to an open, avowed order to murder him. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew more precisely means Saul spoke "about killing David" (so LXX and Syriac), showing his murderous intent had been gradually intensifying — first secret envy, then half-crazed spear-throwing, then dangerous military assignments, and now open talk of assassination. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**Gill** observes that Saul spoke to Jonathan despite knowing his friendship with David, hoping that Jonathan's concern for his own succession to the throne might turn him against David. He also enlisted "all his servants," some of whom may have secretly resented David. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html)

**Spurgeon** (quoted at Precept Austin): "He was now worse than ever, or he would not have spoken to others to aid him in a dastardly murder. When God leaves a man, the devil comes to him." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-19-commentary)

**David Guzik** stresses that Saul created a moral crisis for everyone: Jonathan knew the command violated Exodus 20:13 ("You shall not murder"), and the servants who had previously loved David (1 Sam 18:5) were now ordered to kill him. Jonathan faced the classic dilemma of obeying God rather than men (cf. Acts 5:29). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

---

## vv. 2–3 — Jonathan Warns David and Plans to Intercede

**Traditional reading:** Jonathan, delighting greatly in David, immediately warns him. Gill notes it was likely evening when Jonathan informed David, and he advised hiding until morning when he could approach his father. The plan was for Jonathan to join Saul during his morning walk in the open field, probe his real intentions, and report back. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html) The Pulpit Commentary similarly explains that Jonathan would "stand beside" Saul in the unenclosed hill pastures where the king took his walk, and after the conversation would continue his walk and meet David separately without arousing suspicion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** highlights that Jonathan did not just refuse to participate in evil — he actively helped David. He could have said "I'll stay neutral," but true friendship and godliness demanded more. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

---

## vv. 4–5 — Jonathan's Bold Plea for David

**Traditional reading:** Jonathan speaks "good of David" — not flattery but truth about David's character, loyalty, and valour. Gill lists the specific good works: slaying the Philistines when Israel was terrified, driving away the evil spirit through his harp-playing, and leading troops to victory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html)

**Ellicott** (from the search excerpt) stresses the dramatic irony: "The heir to the throne—the one above all men likely to be injured by the growing popularity of David—with great power and intense earnestness, represented to his father the king the great virtues, the unrivalled gifts, and, above all, the splendid services of the young soldier." He paraphrases Jonathan: "On that ever memorable occasion when he fought the giant … he put his life in his hand. Had he missed a hair's-breadth, the giant would have slain him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/19.htm)

**Pulpit Commentary** notes that Jonathan's argument has three prongs: (a) David has not sinned against Saul — the king's suspicion is unfounded; (b) David's works have been "very good" toward Saul; (c) Saul himself saw Goliath's defeat and rejoiced — so killing David would be sinning against innocent blood without cause. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** adds that Jonathan was essentially telling Saul: "Satan has filled your mind with envy and jealousy. Go back to how you thought before." He notes that Saul had re-coloured the facts — he could not believe David killed Goliath for a righteous reason, instead imagining David was a "grasping traitor." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Baptist perspective (Garner-Howes):** The commentary lists Jonathan's arguments in four pointed points: (1) Saul was sinning against David, but David had not sinned against him; (2) all of David's deeds had been good for Saul; (3) David had risked his life killing Goliath and the king rejoiced; (4) to take David's life would be shedding innocent blood without cause. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-19.html)

---

## vv. 6–7 — Saul's Oath and Temporary Reconciliation

**Traditional reading:** Saul "hearkened unto the voice of Jonathan." Gill says the Lord worked on Saul's mind through Jonathan's words, and Saul was convicted — at least for the present — that he was wrong. Saul swore "As the LORD lives, he shall not be slain." Gill considers it more likely that Saul genuinely intended to keep this oath, though his resolve proved short-lived. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** calls this "real humility" on Saul's part — it would have been easy for the king to say "I'm the king and I'm right." But Saul heeded Jonathan. David was brought back "as in times past." Yet Guzik also notes the ominous foreshadowing: "Saul broke his oath not once but twice, showing how easily a person can abandon their commitments when tempted and spiritually vulnerable." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Clarke** observes that in consequence of this oath, Saul likely "issued orders contrary to those which he had given the preceding day." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_samuel/19.htm)

---

## vv. 8–10 — Renewed War, Renewed Jealousy, and the Spear Again

**Traditional reading:** War breaks out again with the Philistines, and David's military success — striking them "with a mighty blow" — rekindles Saul's jealousy. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the phrase "evil spirit from the LORD" (more correctly "an evil spirit from Jehovah") is the same language as 1 Samuel 16:14, not 18:10 (which used "from God"). The Pulpit suggests this implies Saul, "having broken his covenant relations with Jehovah, was now punished by him" — it was no longer a merely "natural influence." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**Gill** says the evil spirit returned "upon those victories of David," and describes Saul sitting at home with his javelin, suspicious of everyone. David, in humility, was still willing to play the harp to soothe Saul. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** draws a practical lesson: Saul was "unprepared to handle temptation, unprepared to handle spiritual attack, and had the opportunity to sin close at hand. Most of us will trip up under those circumstances." He notes the irony that "the thing Saul didn't need — the spear — was left. The one thing Saul really did need — the person David — was gone." David fled and "never returned to the palace until he was the king of Israel — perhaps some 15 years later." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Ellicott** notes that the "javelin" is the same great spear that appears repeatedly in 1 Samuel as always in Saul's hand or by his side — a symbol of his murderous obsession. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/19.htm)

---

## vv. 11–12 — Michal Helps David Escape Through the Window

**Traditional reading:** Saul surrounds David's house with men ordered to kill him in the morning. Michal, Saul's own daughter, warns David: "If you do not save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be dead!" She lowers him through a window. Gill notes that she may have perceived the danger either by spotting the watchers herself or through a tip from Jonathan or another friend at court. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html) The Pulpit Commentary adds that the watchers were told to wait until morning so David would emerge unsuspecting, making the kill certain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** notes that Michal acted according to the Genesis 2:24 principle — former family loyalties take a back seat to the marriage bond. He also notes the connection to **Psalm 59**, whose superscription says it was composed "when Saul sent men, and they watched the house in order to kill him." David was singing to the LORD even in mortal danger. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Desiring God (John Piper)** connects this chapter to **Psalm 34** as well, noting that David wrote "Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good!" not because he was flooded with blessings but despite his suffering. However, most scholars connect Psalm 34 more directly to 1 Samuel 21 (David before Achish at Gath). (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-will-be-good-again-tomorrow)

---

## v. 13 — Michal's Deception with the Teraphim (Household Idol)

**Traditional reading:** This verse has drawn much comment. The "image" (Hebrew *teraphim*) was a household idol. The Pulpit Commentary describes it as "a wooden block with head and shoulders roughly shaped to represent a human figure" — large enough to pass in a bed for a man. Laban's teraphim were small enough for Rachel to hide under a camel's saddle, but Michal's seems to have been life-sized. The "pillow of goats' hair" is more correctly "a goat's skin about its head" (so Syriac and Vulgate), arranged to look at a distance like a man's hair. The Septuagint reads "goat's liver," based on the idea that a goat's liver palpitated long after death and could mimic a person's breathing — but the Pulpit dismisses this as a different reading without manuscript authority. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** says the presence of the teraphim reveals Michal's "weak relationship with God," noting that "God's people had no business having or using an image like this." He traces this flaw forward to Michal's later contempt for David's worship in 2 Samuel 6:16–23. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Gill** surveys various interpretations: some rabbis thought the teraphim were astrological talismans; others thought they were statues of husbands that wives kept out of love. Gill himself regards them as household gods — unlawful objects that David would not have tolerated had he known of them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html)

---

## vv. 14–17 — The Ruse Discovered; Michal's Lie to Saul

**Traditional reading:** Michal tells the messengers David is sick. Saul, not deceived, orders them to bring David "in the bed" so he can kill David personally — revealing the depth of his hatred. When the deception is discovered, Saul accuses Michal: "Why have you deceived me … and sent my enemy away?" The Pulpit Commentary notes that Michal, afraid of her father's wrath, tells a falsehood: she claims David threatened to kill her if she did not help him escape. The Pulpit adds that "Saul, no doubt, saw that she had been a willing agent; but as she professed to have been driven to do what she had done by David's threats, he could say no more." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**Clarke** notes that Michal's lie was "to excuse herself to her father: as a wife she could do not less than favour the escape of her husband, being perfectly satisfied that there was no guilt in him." He also observes that her falsehood was at the expense of David's reputation — she made him sound like a man who would murder his own wife. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_samuel/19.htm)

**David Guzik** calls Saul's use of the phrase "my enemy" the saddest words in the passage: "David was really Saul's friend … David was only the enemy of Saul because Saul wanted to see him that way." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Gray's Concise Commentary** (from studylight) notes that "Michal's subterfuge is justifiable though its recital in the record is not necessarily a divine approval." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/1-samuel-19.html)

---

## v. 18 — David Flees to Samuel at Ramah/Naioth

**Traditional reading:** David flees to Samuel, the prophet who anointed him. Gill says David came to Samuel "that his faith might be strengthened by him with respect to the kingdom … and that he might have some advice and direction." The Pulpit Commentary notes that there is every reason to believe David had been trained by Samuel among the "sons of the prophets," and now "conscious of his innocence, he flees for refuge to his old master." The word "Naioth" (or Nevayoth) is not a place-name but means "dwellings" or "lodgings" — it is always rendered in the Chaldee Targum as "house of learning" or "house of doctrine." It refers to the residential quarters of Samuel's prophetic school near Ramah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**David Guzik** imagines David pouring out his heart: "Samuel, you anointed me king and look what happened! … Does God want me dead? Why is the LORD allowing this?" He notes that David did the right thing in a confusing situation — he spent time with a godly man. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

---

## vv. 19–21 — Three Waves of Messengers Overcome by the Spirit

**Traditional reading:** Saul sends messengers to arrest David, but when they arrive at Naioth and see the company of prophets prophesying with Samuel presiding over them, the Spirit of God comes upon the messengers and they also prophesy. This happens a second time, then a third. The Pulpit Commentary provides a vivid description: "Samuel himself was standing — not as appointed over them; he was the founder and originator of these schools … and they, full of Divine enthusiasm, were chanting psalms to God's glory. So noble was the sight, that Saul's messengers on entering were seized with a like enthusiasm, and, laying aside their murderous purpose, joined in the hearty service of the prophetic sanctuary." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**Ellicott** quotes Ewald's paraphrase: "They suddenly stood still, spell-bound by the music and solemn dance of the devotees; then, more and more powerfully drawn by the same Spirit into the charmed circle, they broke forth into similar words and gestures; and then, flinging away their upper garments, they … utterly forgot the hostile spirit in which they had come." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/19.htm)

**David Guzik** stresses that the Hebrew word for "prophesying" does not necessarily mean predicting the future — it means speaking under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, likely spontaneous, inspired praise. He adds that this was "the Holy Spirit's warning … 'I don't want David captured. … Instead of seeking to kill David, you should seek to be filled with the Spirit of God.'" Three times God said "Hands off My servant David," yet Saul refused to hear. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**Gray's Concise Commentary** clarifies: "The meaning of 'prophesied' … is more likely that the influence of the sacred exercises produced an effect that made them unable to discharge their commission, led by a resistless impulse to join in praising God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/1-samuel-19.html)

---

## vv. 22–24 — Saul Himself Prophesies, Strips, and Lies Naked

**Traditional reading:** Saul eventually goes himself. He stops at the "great cistern at Secu" (a well-known landmark at the time, now lost) to ask directions. Even before arriving, the Spirit of God comes upon him, and he "walked along prophesying" all the way to Naioth. There he strips off his clothes — understood by most commentators as his royal outer garments (his *beged* and *meil*), not total nudity — and lies prostrate "all that day and all that night." The Pulpit Commentary explains: "His excitement had evidently been intense, and probably to the chanting he had added violent gesticulation. But it was not this so much as the tempest of his emotions which had exhausted him, and made him thus throw himself down as one dead." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**Clarke** says Saul "threw off his royal robes or military dress, retaining only his tunic; and continued so all that day and all that night, uniting with the sons of the prophets in prayers, singing praises, and other religious exercises." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/1_samuel/19.htm)

**David Guzik** interprets the stripping as an expression of deep humility forced upon Saul by God: "Saul would not humble himself before God, and so God would find a way to humble him. … It was a way for the LORD to say, 'You really aren't a king anymore, Saul. I've stripped you of your royal glory.'" He also makes the important distinction: "A person can be affected by the power of God (resulting in amazing experiences), but not surrendered to the power of God, which results in a changed life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

**The proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?"** — First used in 1 Samuel 10:10–12 when Saul's initial anointing produced genuine (though temporary) prophetic enthusiasm. Now the proverb is revived with bitter irony. The Pulpit Commentary: "When first used, Saul's enthusiasm was an outburst of piety, genuine but evanescent, and which had long since passed away. What was it now? The Chaldee, as explained by Rashi, says he was mad." The Pulpit prefers a more sympathetic reading: the thought of seeing Samuel — from whom Saul had been so long estranged — brought back memories of the old days when the prophet had loved and counselled him. "And the remembrance overpowered him. What would he not have given to have continued such as he then was! And for a time he became once again the old Saul of Ramah; but the change was transient and fitful." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

**Ellicott** notes that this passage (1 Sam 19:18 to chapter's end) was appointed by the Church to be read on Whitsun (Pentecost), because of the dramatic outpouring of the Spirit — a foreshadowing of Acts 2. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/19.htm)

**Precept Austin** notes that God's protection of David in this chapter is a "demonstration of God's power, as well as an ironic reminder of Saul's initial call to kingship." Saul began his royal career prophesying among the prophets (1 Sam 10), and now, near the end of his decline, the Spirit seizes him once more — but this time to disarm and humiliate him, not to empower him for service. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-19-commentary)

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The traditional commentaries examined (Gill — Baptist; Guzik — broadly evangelical/Pentecostal-leaning; Pulpit — non-denominational Anglican; Ellicott — Anglican; Clarke — Methodist/Wesleyan; Garner-Howes — Baptist) are largely harmonised on this narrative chapter. Differences are subtle:

- **On the "evil spirit from the LORD" (v. 9):** The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) makes a point of distinguishing "from God" (1 Sam 18:10, a more natural influence) versus "from Jehovah" (here and 1 Sam 16:14, a covenant punishment). Guzik simply treats it as a "distressing spirit." Both agree it is permitted by God's sovereign will. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-19.html)

- **On Michal's deception and the teraphim (v. 13):** Guzik (evangelical/Pentecostal) sees the idol as revealing Michal's weak spiritual life. The Pulpit Commentary treats the teraphim more as a superstitious cultural holdover — widespread despite prophetic teaching — and Michal's ruse as a "pious artifice." Clarke (Methodist) excuses Michal's lie as a wife's necessary protection of her innocent husband, while noting it came at David's expense. Gray's Concise Commentary explicitly says the deception is "justifiable though its recital in the record is not necessarily a divine approval." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/1-samuel-19.html)

- **On Saul's prophesying (vv. 23–24):** Reformed-influenced teachers (like Guzik, who draws on Spurgeon and Poole) emphasise that this "amazing experience" was not a changed life — an important distinction in traditions that stress perseverance and genuine regeneration. Guzik: "A person can be affected by the power of God … but not surrendered to the power of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-19/)

- **On Saul's oath (v. 6):** Gill (Baptist, Calvinistic) inclines toward Saul's sincerity: "the former seems rather to be the case" that Saul genuinely intended to keep the oath. Guzik also treats it as a genuine work of the LORD on Saul's heart. Both agree the repentance was temporary — a cautionary tale about the instability of unregenerate resolves. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-19.html)
